chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdillah from his uncle Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah from Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn 'Ammar who said:

I said to al-Rida (peace be upon him): A man has money that is due to its owner; he sells it for a pearl worth one hundred dirhams for one thousand dirhams, and delays the money from him until a specified time. He (al-Rida) said: 'There is no harm in it. My father ordered me to do so, and I did that.' And he claimed that he asked Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) about it, and he said the same thing.

key_terms.أَبَا اَلْحَسَنِ مُوسَى: Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), Imam Musa al-Kazim
key_terms.اَلرِّضَا: Al-Rida (peace be upon him), the 8th Imam
key_terms.اَلْمَالُ: Money/wealth, specifically referring to a debt here
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (permissible)
key_terms.لُؤْلُؤَةً: A pearl, used here as a metaphor for the debt instrument or the transaction object

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sell a debt for more than its face value with delayed payment in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* validates the practice of selling a debt for a higher price with deferred payment, a key mechanism in Islamic finance known as *bay' al-dayn bi-ziyadah*. Imam al-Rida (AS) confirms its perecessibility by citing his father, Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS), establishing a continuous chain of authority (*tawatur*) within the Ahl al-Bayt that supports this commercial transaction. This ruling distinguishes the sale of debt from *riba* (usury) by treating the profit as compensation for the delay in payment rather than interest on the principal.
